Show the PC screen as a virtual screen for a phone VR viewer (Cardboard). Tap the screen, or press the viewer\'s button, to bring the screen back in front of you.

Shows HDR games as real HDR on the phone\'s screen, like your TV, instead of converting them to a normal picture: brighter highlights and the game\'s full colors. The screen stays in HDR mode for the whole stream (brighter, more heat). Color, Contrast and Color space still apply (Native stretches the colors to the screen\'s full range, like a TV\'s Native mode), and HDR highlights limits how bright whites get. Highlight compression doesn\'t apply, and HDR white level sets how bright the desktop and other normal pictures are.

For HDR on the phone\'s screen. In a headset, very bright whites glare through the lenses and make the rest of the picture look pale. This limits how bright whites get and brightens the mid-tones a little, so grass, kits and the crowd look richer. Softer steps are easier on the eyes and run cooler.
Full: as the game sends them
Inside a headset the phone\'s light sensor is covered, so automatic brightness dims the screen and colors look dull. This holds the brightness while streaming. Brighter means more heat.

For HDR games: how bright the game\'s white is. Lower makes the picture brighter but flattens bright areas; higher keeps more contrast and color in bright areas (sky, lit grass, the crowd) but darkens the rest. Games set up for a bright TV often look best at 250–300.
For HDR games: how much of the picture stays untouched before the brightest parts are squeezed to fit the phone. Punchy keeps more contrast; Soft keeps more detail in the very brightest highlights.
Color saturation, like a TV\'s Color control. 100% is accurate; higher makes colors stronger.
The display gamma to imitate. 2.2 is accurate for the phone; 2.4 gives deeper mid-tones and richer colors, like a TV in a dark room.
Gamma 2.4 (deeper, like a TV in a dark room)

Shows the game\'s frames at the steady pace the PC made them, instead of each one the moment it\'s decoded, so small timing wobbles on the network or in the decoder don\'t show up as stutter. A bigger buffer absorbs bigger hiccups but delays the picture a little more. Head tracking isn\'t delayed.
Off: show each frame at once

How HDR colors are shown. Native uses the screen\'s full color range, like a TV\'s Native color space, so the most saturated colors aren\'t cut off; it needs the phone\'s Screen mode on Vivid. Auto converts to standard sRGB colors; pick it with Screen mode on Natural. With HDR on the phone\'s screen, Native stretches the game\'s colors to the screen\'s full range (the phone itself shows HDR accurately, which looks less vivid than a TV), and Auto keeps them accurate.
Native: the screen\'s full color range

Always stream at 1920×1080 with HDR, at about 50 Mbps at 60 FPS, the way EA SPORTS FC 27 runs fullscreen. The stream doesn\'t follow the PC\'s resolution, so starting or leaving the game doesn\'t reconnect it; the 4K desktop is shown at 1080p. Overrides Resolution, Bitrate and Enable HDR, and turns off \"Resolution: match the PC\".

Stream at the resolution the PC\'s screen is in, so a fullscreen game at 1080p is streamed at 1080p instead of being enlarged to 4K. The bitrate follows: 1080p about 50, 1440p about 80, 4K about 100 Mbps. When a game changes resolution, the stream reconnects for a second or two. Needs the VR Desktop Host app on the PC; without it, the Resolution and Bitrate settings apply.
The lens type of the headset the phone sits in
Cardboard v2 and most plastic viewers
cardoO VR Go (turn its IPD dial until the image is single)

For viewers with an IPD dial: set the distance between the lenses. If the image doubles or won\'t come into focus after you turn the dial, the app\'s lens distance doesn\'t match it. cardoO VR Go: 60 mm with the lenses at their closest, 70 mm at their widest.

For viewers with a focus dial. Turn the dial until text is sharp, then pick the value here at which the screen stays still when you turn your head: if it drifts the way you turn, pick a bigger number; if it drifts the other way, a smaller one. Judge it on the middle of the screen. cardoO VR Go: about 37.5 mm with the lenses closest to the phone, 46.5 mm farthest.
How wide the PC screen looks, in degrees of your view. Bigger makes text easier to read; smaller fits the whole screen in view.

For 3D movies and games that the PC shows as two pictures, side by side or one above the other. Each eye sees its own picture, stretched back to the full screen, so the picture has depth. Keep it Off for the normal desktop, or each eye sees only half of it. If the depth looks inside out, pick \'right eye first\'.
This phone has no rotation sensor, so the virtual screen can\'t stay in place when you move your head.

Puts picture quality ahead of speed and battery. Turns on High-quality scaling and Anti screen-door and keeps 4K frames at full size, whatever those switches say. Picture softness and Sharpness stay as you set them.

The stream has more pixels than the phone can show on the virtual screen, so it\'s shrunk to fit. This reads the picture four times per screen pixel instead of once: less shimmer and false detail on grass, nets, the crowd and text, and a truer picture. Costs more graphics work.

Makes the pixel grid stand out less. The phone\'s screen has half as many red and blue subpixels as green ones, so sharp color detail sparkles and shows a colored mesh through the lenses. This softens only the color of fine detail and keeps brightness, and so text, sharp; Sharpness then sharpens brightness only. The black gaps between pixels are physical: a matte screen protector hides them best, with Sharpness to win back detail.
Sharpens the PC screen to make up for the softening of the lenses and the downscale. Try 30–50%; too much adds halos around text.

How smoothly the stream is shrunk onto the virtual screen. Higher is smoother, with a less visible pixel grid and less sparkle on fine detail; lower is crisper for small text. 0% is the sharpest. Try 70–90% for games.

Shrinks a stream much larger than one eye\'s part of the screen (4K) to half its size before drawing it. A quarter of the graphics work per video frame; measured the same picture at higher Picture softness, slightly softer at low softness.
Keep the virtual screen in place when you turn your head. Turn off to keep the screen fixed in front of your eyes.
A tap puts the screen where you\'re looking, higher or lower too (for example when you lean back). Off keeps it at eye level and only turns it left or right.
How often the view is redrawn. Higher is smoother when you turn your head; lower saves battery and heat. Above 60 Hz on Samsung phones needs Settings → Display → Motion smoothness → Adaptive.
Records how each frame gets from the PC to the screen, and why any stutters, to a file on the phone (about 5–10 MB an hour; the last 15 streams are kept). For finding stutter; see docs/FRAME-LOG.md.
Show a panel below the virtual screen with the network status (green OK, yellow unstable, red poor), the PC\'s encode time and the phone\'s decode time. Look down to read it.
%1$d Hz isn\'t available, so the view runs at %2$d Hz. On Samsung phones, set Settings → Display → Motion smoothness to Adaptive.
